In [[mathematics]], the '''Jabotinsky matrix''' (sometimes called '''iteration matrix''' or '''power matrix''') is an [[infinite matrix]] used to convert [[function composition]] into [[matrix multiplication]]. It is often used in [[iteration theory]] to find the continuous [[Iterated function|iteration of functions]]. The matrix is named after mathematician [[Eri Jabotinsky]].

==Definition==
Let <math>f</math> be a [[formal power series]]. There exists coefficients <math>(B_{n,k})_{n, k\geq 0}</math> such that<math display="block">f(x)^k = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} B_{n,k} x^n.</math>The '''Jabotinsky matrix''' of <math>f(x)</math> is defined as the infinite matrix<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Comtet |first=Louis |title=Advanced Combinatorics: The Art of Finite and Infinite Expansions |date=1974 |publisher=Springer Netherlands |isbn=978-94-010-2198-2 |location=Dordrecht}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Knuth |first=D. |year=1992 |title=Convolution Polynomials |journal=The Mathematica Journal |volume=2 |issue=4 |pages=67–78 |arxiv=math/9207221 |bibcode=1992math......7221K}}</ref>
:<math>\mathbf B(f) = \left(\begin{array}{cccc}
B_{0,0} & B_{0,1} & B_{0,2} & \cdots \\
B_{1,0} & B_{1,1} & B_{1,2} & \cdots \\
B_{2,0} & B_{2,1} & B_{2,2} & \cdots \\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots
\end{array}\right).</math>
When <math>f(0) = 0</math>, <math>\mathbf B(f)</math> becomes an infinite lower [[triangular matrix]] whose entries are given by [[Bell polynomials#Ordinary Bell polynomials|ordinary Bell polynomials]] evaluated at the coefficients of <math>f</math>. This is why <math>\mathbf B(f)</math> is sometimes referred to as a ''Bell matrix''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Aldrovandi |first=R. |last2=Freitas |first2=L. P. |date=1998-10-01 |title=Continuous iteration of dynamical maps |url=https://pubs.aip.org/jmp/article/39/10/5324/309077/Continuous-iteration-of-dynamical-maps |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |language=en |volume=39 |issue=10 |pages=5324–5336 |doi=10.1063/1.532574 |issn=0022-2488|arxiv=physics/9712026 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Aldrovandi |first=R. |title=Special matrices of mathematical physics: stochastic, circulant, and Bell matrices |date=2001 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-02-4708-9 |location=Singapore ; River Edge, N.J}}</ref>

== History ==
Jabotinsky matrices have a long history, and were perhaps used for the first time in the context  of [[iteration theory]] by Albert A. Bennett<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bennett |first=Albert A. |date=1915 |title=The Iteration of Functions of one Variable |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2007213?origin=crossref |journal=The Annals of Mathematics |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=23 |doi=10.2307/2007213|url-access=subscription }}</ref> in 1915. Jabotinsky later pursued Bennett's research<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jabotinsky |first=Eri |year=1947 |title=Sur la représentation de la composition de fonctions par un produit de matrices. Applicaton à l'itération de e^x et de e^x-1. |journal=Comptes rendus de l'Académie des Sciences |volume=224 |pages=323–324}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jabotinsky |first=Eri |date=1955 |title=Iterational invariants |url=https://mathscinet.ams.org/mathscinet/article?mr=74530 |journal=Technion. Israel Institute of Technology. Scientific Publications |volume=6 |pages=64-80}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Erdös |first1=Paul |authorlink1=Paul Erdős |last2=Jabotinsky |first2=Eri | authorlink2=Eri Jabotinsky |date=1960 |title=On analytic iteration |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF02786856 |journal=[[Journal d'Analyse Mathématique]] |language=en |volume=8 |issue=1 |pages=361–376 |doi=10.1007/BF02786856 |issn=0021-7670|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Jabotinsky |first=Eri |date=1963 |title=Analytic iteration |url=https://www.ams.org/tran/1963-108-03/S0002-9947-1963-0155971-X/ |journal=Transactions of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=108 |issue=3 |pages=457–477 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9947-1963-0155971-X |issn=0002-9947}}</ref> and applied them to [[Faber polynomials]]<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Jabotinsky |first=Eri |authorlink=Eri Jabotinsky |date=1953 |title=Representation of functions by matrices. Application to Faber polynomials |journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]] |language=en |volume=4 |issue=4 |pages=546–553 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1953-0059359-0 |issn=0002-9939 |doi-access=free}}</ref>. Jabotinsky matrices were popularized during the 70s by {{interlanguage link|Louis Comtet|fr}}'s book ''Advanced Combinatorics'', where he referred to them as ''iteration matrices'' (which is a denomination also sometimes used nowadays<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Aschenbrenner |first=Matthias |date=2012 |title=Logarithms of iteration matrices, and proof of a conjecture by Shadrin and Zvonkine |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] |series=Series A |language=en |volume=119 |issue=3 |pages=627–654 |doi=10.1016/j.jcta.2011.11.008|doi-access=free }}</ref>). This article's denomination appeared later<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lavoie |first=J. L. |last2=Tremblay |first2=R. |date=1981 |title=The Jabotinsky Matrix of a Power Series |url=http://epubs.siam.org/doi/10.1137/0512067 |journal=SIAM Journal on Mathematical Analysis |language=en |volume=12 |issue=6 |pages=819–825 |doi=10.1137/0512067 |issn=0036-1410|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Brini |first=Andrea |date=1984-05-01 |title=Higher dimensional recursive matrices and diagonal delta sets of series |journal=[[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] |series=Series A |volume=36 |issue=3 |pages=315–331 |doi=10.1016/0097-3165(84)90039-6 |issn=0097-3165|doi-access=free}}</ref>'''<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lang |first=W. |year=2000 |title=On generalizations of the stirling number triangles |journal=Journal of Integer Sequences |volume=3 |issue=2.4 |pages=1–19 |bibcode=2000JIntS...3...24L}}</ref>'''<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Mansour |first=Toufik |last2=Schork |first2=Matthias |last3=Shattuck |first3=Mark |date=2012-11-01 |title=On the Stirling numbers associated with the meromorphic Weyl algebra |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893965912000808 |journal=Applied Mathematics Letters |volume=25 |issue=11 |pages=1767–1771 |doi=10.1016/j.aml.2012.02.009 |issn=0893-9659|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sokal |first=Alan D. |date=2023-02-01 |title=Total positivity of some polynomial matrices that enumerate labeled trees and forests I: forests of rooted labeled trees |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/s00605-022-01687-0 |journal=Monatshefte für Mathematik |language=en |volume=200 |issue=2 |pages=389–452 |doi=10.1007/s00605-022-01687-0 |issn=1436-5081|arxiv=2105.05583 }}</ref>. [[Donald Knuth]] uses the name ''convolution matrix''.<ref name=":1" />

==Properties==
Jabotinsky matrices satisfy the fundamental relationship<math display="block">\textbf B(f \circ g) = \textbf B(g)\textbf B(f)</math>which makes the Jabotinsky matrix <math>\mathbf B(f)</math> a (direct) representation of <math>f(x)</math>. Here the term <math>f \circ g </math> denotes the [[Function composition|composition]] of functions <math>f(g(x))</math>.

The fundamental property implies
*<math>\textbf B(f^n) = \textbf B(f)^n</math>, where <math>f^n</math> is an [[iterated function]] and <math>n</math> is a [[natural number]].
*<math>\textbf B(f^{-1}) = \textbf B(f)^{-1}</math>, where <math>f^{-1}</math> is the [[inverse function]], if <math>f</math> has a [[Formal power series#Composition inverse|compositional inverse]].
*<math> \begin{bmatrix}1,x,x^2,...\end{bmatrix} \textbf B(f) = \begin{bmatrix}1,f(x),f(x)^2,...\end{bmatrix}. </math>

==Generalization==
Given a sequence <math>(\Omega_n)_{n\ge0}</math>, we can instead define the matrix with the coefficient <math>(B_{n,k}^\Omega)_{n, k\geq 0}</math> by<ref name=":0" /><math display="block">\Omega_k f(x)^k = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} B^\Omega_{n,k} \Omega_n x^n.</math>If <math>(\Omega_n)_{n\ge0}</math> is the constant sequence equal to <math>1</math>, we recover Jabotinsky matrices. In some contexts, the sequence is chosen to be <math>\Omega_n = 1/n!</math>, so that the entry are given by regular [[Bell polynomials]]. This is a more convenient form for functions such as <math>f(x) = -\log(1-x)</math> and <math>f(x) = e^x - 1</math> where [[Stirling number|Stirling numbers of the first and second kind]] appear in the matrices (see the examples).

This generalization gives a completely equivalent matrix since <math>B_{n,k}^\Omega \frac{\Omega_n}{\Omega_k} = B_{n,k}</math>.

==Examples==

* The Jabotinsky matrix of a constant is:
*:<math>\mathbf B(a) = \left(\begin{array}{cccc}
1&a&a^2& \cdots \\
0&0&0& \cdots \\
0&0&0& \cdots \\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots
\end{array}\right)</math>
* The Jabotinsky matrix of a constant multiple is:
*:<math>\textbf B(cx) = \left(\begin{array}{cccc}
1&0&0& \cdots \\
0&c&0& \cdots \\
0&0&c^2& \cdots \\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots
\end{array}\right)</math>
* The Jabotinsky matrix of the [[successor function]]:
*:<math>\textbf B(1+x) = \left(\begin{array}{ccccc}
1&1&1&1& \cdots \\
0&1&2&3& \cdots \\
0&0&1&3& \cdots \\
0&0&0&1& \cdots \\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots
\end{array}\right)</math>
*:The matrix displays [[Pascal's triangle]].
*The Jabotinsky matrix of the [[exponential function]] is given by <math>\textbf B(\exp)_{n,k} = \frac{k^n}{n!}</math>.
* The Jabotinsky matrix of the [[logarithm]] is related to the (unsigned) [[Stirling numbers of the first kind]] scaled by [[factorial]]s:
*:<math>\textbf B(-\log(1 - x)) = \left(\begin{array}{cccccc}
1&0&0&0&0& \cdots \\
0&1&0&0&0& \cdots \\
0&\frac{1}{2}&1&0&0& \cdots \\
0&\frac{1}{3}&1&1&0& \cdots \\
0&\frac{1}{4}&\frac{11}{12}&\frac{3}{2}&1& \cdots \\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots
\end{array}\right)</math>
*:<math>\textbf B(-\log(1 - x))_{n, k} = \left[{n \atop k}\right] \frac{k!}{n!}</math>
* The Jabotinsky matrix of the exponential function minus 1 is related to the [[Stirling numbers of the second kind]] scaled by factorials:
*:<math>\textbf B(\exp(x) - 1) = \left(\begin{array}{cccccc}
1&0&0&0&0& \cdots \\
0&1&0&0&0& \cdots \\
0&\frac{1}{2}&1&0&0& \cdots \\
0&\frac{1}{6}&1&1&0& \cdots \\
0&\frac{1}{24}&\frac{7}{12}&\frac{3}{2}&1& \cdots \\
\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\ddots
\end{array}\right)</math>
*:<math>\textbf B(\exp(x) - 1)_{n,k} = \left\{{n \atop k}\right\} \frac{k!}{n!}</math>

== Alternative convention ==
Some authors,<ref name=":4" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Schippers |first=Eric |date=2006 |title=The Power Matrix, coadjoint action and quadratic differentials |url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF02790277 |journal=[[Journal d'Analyse Mathématique]] |language=en |volume=98 |issue=1 |pages=249–277 |doi=10.1007/BF02790277 |issn=0021-7670|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":3" /> which include Bennett and Jabotinsky in their original work, use the [[transpose]] convention <math>\mathbf B(f)^{\text{T}}</math> for the matrix, which is an infinite upper [[triangular matrix]] when <math>f(0) = 0</math>. The fundamental relationship becomes<math display="block">\textbf B(f \circ g)^{\text{T}} = \textbf B(f)^{\text{T}}\textbf B(g)^{\text{T}},</math>which preserves the order of the operations.

==Related matrices==

* Jabotinsky matrices are a special case of the later introduced [[Riordan array]]s.
* They are also related to [[Carleman linearization]] and ''Carleman (embedding) matrices.''<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tsiligiannis |first=C. A |last2=Lyberatos |first2=G |date=1987-08-15 |title=Steady state bifurcations and exact multiplicity conditions via Carleman linearization |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/0022247X87900825 |journal=Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications |volume=126 |issue=1 |pages=143–160 |doi=10.1016/0022-247X(87)90082-5 |issn=0022-247X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Kowalski |first=Krzysztof |title=Nonlinear dynamical systems and Carleman linearization |last2=Steeb |first2=W.-H. |date=1991 |publisher=World Scientific |isbn=978-981-02-0587-4 |location=Singapore ; Teaneck, N.J}}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Gralewicz |first=P. |last2=Kowalski |first2=K. |date=2002 |title=Continuous time evolution from iterated maps and Carleman linearization |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0960077901002223 |journal=Chaos, Solitons & Fractals |language=en |volume=14 |issue=4 |pages=563–572 |doi=10.1016/S0960-0779(01)00222-3|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* [[Grunsky matrix|Grunsky matrices]] can be expressed with Jabotinsky matrices.<ref name=":2" />
